strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: converting naturally occurring conversational feedback into preference supervision. The construction of 20,281 expert-generated preference pairs, alongside policy-specific variants, is a useful practical contribution.

Experiments cover three model families, two response-generation strategies, and three established benchmarks. Improvements over the starting models are substantial: Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate rises from 24.3% to 34.9%, and its Arena-Hard score from 15.4% to 32.4%. These results support the pipeline’s utility beyond the proposed internal evaluation.

Human validation covers feedback detection on 50 conversations and checklist evaluation on 200 conversations. Reporting agreement, using length-controlled evaluation, and separating training and test users and conversations are valuable methodological safeguards.

The pipeline is understandable, and the appendices provide detailed rubrics, major prompts, model identities, and SFT/DPO hyperparameters. The limitations explicitly acknowledge selection bias and potentially harmful user preferences.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the value of user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. Regenerating responses with matching models does not remove these confounds. A baseline using the same WildChat prompts without feedback conditioning, with comparable filtering and training budgets, is needed to establish the central attribution. An SFT-only comparison would also clarify the contribution of preference optimization.

The claim that checklist evaluation more accurately reflects actual users is only partially supported. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates or filters training responses, and evaluates outputs against those preferences, creating a risk of correlated errors. The human audit reports 57.14% agreement and kappa 0.372, compared with human–human kappa 0.436; it does not establish that checklists improve agreement over unguided evaluation or report human win rates for the trained-model comparisons. Independent validation against the original feedback would strengthen this central claim.

The internal test deliberately selects similar preferences within 70 clusters and tasks resembling training tasks. This supports evaluation on curated, common preferences, but clustering does not establish population-majority preferences or coverage of diverse users. Feedback detection also has only 48.4% DSAT recall. A randomly sampled held-out evaluation and breakdowns by preference type would better establish scope. Claims about addressing bias, subjectivity, and evolving user needs exceed the reported evidence.

The claims of significant and consistent superiority over UltraFeedback are overstated. Table 3 includes exceptions: Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several positive differences are small, and no confidence intervals, significance tests, or training-seed variability are reported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful training details. The manuscript says the dataset will be available soon and supplies no construction-code or dataset link. It also omits the embedding model and sufficient clustering/deduplication specifications, generation decoding settings, and the validation protocol used for hyperparameter selection. Together with the unresolved attribution and evaluation concerns, these gaps leave the paper borderline for Findings despite its promising empirical results.
